chapters.title: Unit 1: Introduction to DBMS
chapters.content:
Unit 1: Introduction to Database Systems

9 Marks

What is a Database?

A database is an organized collection of structured data stored and accessed electronically. Think of it as a very sophisticated filing cabinet — data is stored in a way that makes retrieval, update, and management efficient.

Real-world example: Your college has a database storing student records (roll no, name, marks, attendance), course details, teacher information, fee payments — all interrelated and queryable.

Traditional File System vs DBMS

File-Based System Problems

  • Data Redundancy: Same data stored in multiple files. Student name in admission file, library file, exam file separately — all must be updated separately.
  • Data Inconsistency: Different files have different values for the same data (student name spelled differently in different files)
  • Data Isolation: Data scattered in different formats — hard to write programs that access multiple files
  • Integrity Problems: Hard to enforce constraints (e.g., age must be > 18)
  • Concurrent Access Issues: Two people updating same file simultaneously causes corruption
  • Security Problems: Hard to restrict who sees what in flat files

DBMS Advantages Over File System

IssueFile SystemDBMS
RedundancyHigh — data duplicatedMinimal — normalized storage
ConsistencyManual, error-proneAutomatic via constraints
SecurityFile-level onlyRow/column level permissions
ConcurrencyNo built-in controlLocking, transactions
Backup/RecoveryManualAutomatic with logging
QueryWrite custom programSQL — standard language

Role of DBA (Database Administrator)

The DBA is responsible for:

  • Designing the database schema
  • Defining access rights and security policies
  • Performance tuning and optimization
  • Backup and recovery planning
  • Managing storage and capacity
  • Keeping DBMS software updated

ANSI-SPARC Architecture — 3-Level Architecture

This is the most important conceptual framework in DBMS. It separates the database into 3 levels to achieve data independence.

Users/Applications
      ↕
  EXTERNAL LEVEL (View Level)
  "What each user sees"
      ↕
CONCEPTUAL LEVEL (Logical Level)
  "What data exists and how it's related"
      ↕
  INTERNAL LEVEL (Physical Level)
  "How data is actually stored"
      ↕
  Actual Physical Storage

External Level (View Level)

Each user or user group sees a customized view of the database. A student sees their marks and attendance. A teacher sees all student marks for their course. The accounts department sees fee payments. Each is a different view of the same underlying data.

Conceptual Level (Logical Level)

Describes what data is stored and the relationships between data. This is the DBA's view — the complete logical structure. Contains: entity definitions, attributes, constraints, relationships.

Internal Level (Physical Level)

Describes how data is physically stored on storage devices. Includes: file organization, index structures, data compression, encryption, record placement.

Data Independence

  • Logical Data Independence: Changes to conceptual schema don't require changes to external schema (add a new column → existing user views aren't broken)
  • Physical Data Independence: Changes to internal schema don't require changes to conceptual schema (move data to SSD → queries still work the same)

Data Models

ModelDescriptionExample
HierarchicalTree structure, parent-childIBM IMS (1960s)
NetworkGraph structure, many-to-manyCODASYL (1970s)
RelationalTables with rows and columnsMySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle
Object-OrientedObjects with methodsObjectDB
NoSQLDocument, key-value, graphMongoDB, Redis, Neo4j

Schemas and Instances

  • Schema: The structure/definition of the database (blueprint). Like the design of a form — the fields. Rarely changes.
  • Instance: The actual data stored at a particular moment. Like the filled-in forms. Changes constantly.
Schema: Student(rollNo INT, name VARCHAR(50), marks FLOAT)
Instance (at 10am): (101, 'Aayan', 95.5), (102, 'Riya', 88.0)
Instance (at 11am): (101, 'Aayan', 96.0)  ← marks updated, schema unchanged

Exam Q&A — Unit 1

Q1: Compare file-based system with DBMS. (6 marks)

Answer: Use the comparison table above. Key points: DBMS eliminates redundancy through normalization, ensures consistency through constraints, provides concurrent access through locking, offers declarative querying through SQL, and provides role-based security.

Q2: Explain the ANSI-SPARC 3-level architecture. (6 marks)

Answer: Three levels: External (user views — each user sees tailored subset), Conceptual (complete logical structure — tables, relationships, constraints), Internal (physical storage details — files, indexes). Separation achieves data independence: changes at one level don't cascade to others.

chapters.title: Unit 2: DB Concepts & Architecture
chapters.content:
Unit 2: Database System Concepts and Architecture

9 Marks

Data Independence (Deep Dive)

Why Data Independence Matters

Imagine you have 500 application programs that query your database. If you change the physical storage (move from HDD to SSD, change index type), should all 500 programs need to be rewritten? No! That's what data independence provides.

Types of Data Independence

Logical Data Independence Example:
  BEFORE: Student(rollNo, name, marks)
  AFTER:  Student(rollNo, name, marks, attendance)
  
  Old views that only select rollNo, name, marks still work fine.
  The application programs are not affected.

Physical Data Independence Example:
  BEFORE: Data stored in B-Tree index
  AFTER:  Data stored in Hash index (for faster equality searches)
  
  SQL queries still work: SELECT * FROM Student WHERE marks > 90;
  The conceptual/external levels are unaffected.

Database System Architecture

Centralized Architecture

All data and DBMS on one machine. Simple but single point of failure. Used in: small businesses, personal databases.

Client-Server Architecture

Client (Application)    ←→    Server (DBMS)
  - Sends SQL queries          - Processes queries
  - Displays results           - Manages data
  - User interface             - Enforces security

Examples: MySQL server + PHP/Python client
          Oracle DB + Java application

Distributed Database Architecture

Data spread across multiple physical locations. Provides high availability and scalability. Used by: Google, Amazon, Facebook.

Client → Site A (Mumbai) ← → Site B (Delhi) ← → Site C (Bangalore)
         (partial data)        (partial data)      (partial data)
         All sites cooperate transparently to serve queries

Database Languages

DDL — Data Definition Language

Defines the structure of the database (schema).

-- Create table
CREATE TABLE Students (
    rollNo INT PRIMARY KEY,
    name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    email VARCHAR(100) UNIQUE,
    marks FLOAT CHECK(marks >= 0 AND marks <= 100),
    dept VARCHAR(30) DEFAULT 'Computer Science'
);

-- Alter table (add column)
ALTER TABLE Students ADD COLUMN phone VARCHAR(15);

-- Drop table
DROP TABLE Students;

-- Truncate (delete all data, keep structure)
TRUNCATE TABLE Students;

DML — Data Manipulation Language

Manipulates data within tables.

-- INSERT
INSERT INTO Students VALUES (101, 'Aayan', 'aayan@hpu.ac.in', 95.5, 'CS');
INSERT INTO Students (rollNo, name, marks) VALUES (102, 'Riya', 88.0);

-- SELECT (most important!)
SELECT * FROM Students;
SELECT name, marks FROM Students WHERE marks > 90;
SELECT name, marks FROM Students ORDER BY marks DESC;
SELECT dept, AVG(marks) FROM Students GROUP BY dept;

-- UPDATE
UPDATE Students SET marks = 96.0 WHERE rollNo = 101;
UPDATE Students SET marks = marks * 1.05;  -- 5% bonus to everyone

-- DELETE
DELETE FROM Students WHERE marks < 30;  -- fail cases
DELETE FROM Students;  -- deletes ALL rows (dangerous!)

DCL — Data Control Language

GRANT SELECT, INSERT ON Students TO 'teacher_user'@'localhost';
REVOKE INSERT ON Students FROM 'teacher_user'@'localhost';

-- Roles
CREATE ROLE 'read_only';
GRANT SELECT ON university.* TO 'read_only';
GRANT 'read_only' TO 'student_user'@'localhost';

TCL — Transaction Control Language

BEGIN;  -- or START TRANSACTION
UPDATE Accounts SET balance = balance - 5000 WHERE id = 1;  -- debit
UPDATE Accounts SET balance = balance + 5000 WHERE id = 2;  -- credit
COMMIT;  -- make it permanent (both succeed)

-- or if something goes wrong:
ROLLBACK;  -- undo all changes (neither debit nor credit applied)

Mappings Between Levels

  • External/Conceptual Mapping: Transforms user view to conceptual schema (e.g., view on a subset of columns)
  • Conceptual/Internal Mapping: Transforms conceptual schema to physical storage (e.g., which columns are indexed)

Exam Q&A — Unit 2

Q1: What is logical vs physical data independence? Why is it important?

Answer: Logical independence: adding/modifying conceptual schema doesn't break existing external views/programs. Physical independence: changing storage structures doesn't break conceptual queries. Importance: allows database evolution without rewriting all application code — critical for large systems.

Q2: Differentiate DDL, DML, DCL, and TCL with examples.

Answer: DDL: CREATE, ALTER, DROP — defines structure. DML: INSERT, SELECT, UPDATE, DELETE — manipulates data. DCL: GRANT, REVOKE — controls access. TCL: COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT — manages transactions.

chapters.title: Unit 3: Relational Model & ER
chapters.content:
Unit 3: Relational and ER Models

12 Marks

Relational Model Concepts

The relational model (proposed by E.F. Codd in 1970) organizes data as a collection of relations (tables).

Key Terminology

Formal TermCommon TermMeaning
RelationTableA 2D table of data
TupleRow/RecordOne record in the table
AttributeColumn/FieldA property of the relation
DomainData type + valid valuesSet of valid values for an attribute
DegreeNumber of columnsHow many attributes
CardinalityNumber of rowsHow many tuples
STUDENT Relation:
┌────────┬──────────┬───────┬────────────────┐
│ RollNo │ Name     │ Marks │ Department     │
├────────┼──────────┼───────┼────────────────┤
│ 101    │ Aayan    │ 95.5  │ CS             │  ← tuple
│ 102    │ Riya     │ 88.0  │ IT             │
│ 103    │ Rohan    │ 76.5  │ CS             │
└────────┴──────────┴───────┴────────────────┘
  ↑ attribute

Degree = 4 (columns)
Cardinality = 3 (rows)

Keys — The Most Important Concept in RDBMS

Super Key

Any set of attributes that uniquely identifies a tuple. Can include extra attributes.

Student(RollNo, Name, Phone, Email)
Super keys: {RollNo}, {Email}, {Phone}, {RollNo, Name}, {RollNo, Name, Phone}, etc.
(Any combination that includes a unique attribute is a super key)

Candidate Key

A minimal super key — no attribute can be removed and still have uniqueness.

Candidate keys: {RollNo}, {Email}, {Phone}
(None of these can be further reduced)

Primary Key

The candidate key selected by the DBA to uniquely identify tuples. Cannot be NULL. Cannot be duplicated.

Primary Key: RollNo  ← chosen from candidate keys

Foreign Key

An attribute in one table that references the primary key of another table. Enforces referential integrity.

STUDENT(RollNo*, Name, DeptCode)   * = Primary Key
DEPARTMENT(DeptCode*, DeptName)

DeptCode in STUDENT is a Foreign Key referencing DEPARTMENT.DeptCode

Rule: Every value of DeptCode in STUDENT must exist in DEPARTMENT.DeptCode
      You cannot add a student with DeptCode='PHYSICS' if that dept doesn't exist.

Alternate Key

Candidate keys that were NOT chosen as primary key.

Composite Key

A primary key made of two or more attributes.

ENROLLMENT(StudentID, CourseID, EnrollDate)
Primary Key: (StudentID, CourseID) — composite key
One student can enroll in many courses, one course has many students
But each (student, course) combination is unique

Entity-Relationship (ER) Model

The ER model is a high-level conceptual data model used to design databases before implementation.

ER Diagram Components

SymbolRepresentsExample
RectangleEntity (strong)STUDENT, COURSE
Dashed rectangleWeak entityDEPENDENT (of an employee)
EllipseAttributename, rollNo, marks
Double ellipseMultivalued attributephone_numbers (can have many)
Dashed ellipseDerived attributeage (derived from date_of_birth)
DiamondRelationshipENROLLS, TEACHES
Double diamondIdentifying relationshipWeak entity's relationship
Underlined attrKey attributerollNo

Strong vs Weak Entities

  • Strong Entity: Has its own primary key. Exists independently. (e.g., STUDENT, EMPLOYEE)
  • Weak Entity: Depends on a strong entity for identity. Has only a partial key. (e.g., DEPENDENT depends on EMPLOYEE — a dependent 'Riya' has no meaning without knowing whose dependent)

Relationships and Cardinality

ONE-TO-ONE (1:1):
  One person has one passport. One passport belongs to one person.
  PERSON ──1── has ──1── PASSPORT

ONE-TO-MANY (1:N):
  One teacher teaches many courses. Each course taught by one teacher.
  TEACHER ──1── teaches ──N── COURSE

MANY-TO-MANY (M:N):
  A student enrolls in many courses. A course has many students.
  STUDENT ──M── enrolls ──N── COURSE
  (Needs a junction/bridge table: ENROLLMENT)

ER Diagram Example: University Database

Entities: STUDENT, COURSE, DEPARTMENT, FACULTY
Relationships:
  STUDENT ---[ENROLLS]--- COURSE        (M:N)
  STUDENT ---[BELONGS_TO]--- DEPARTMENT (N:1)
  FACULTY ---[TEACHES]--- COURSE        (1:N)
  FACULTY ---[WORKS_IN]--- DEPARTMENT   (N:1)

STUDENT attributes: rollNo(key), name, email, phone(multivalued), age(derived)
COURSE attributes:  courseCode(key), title, credits
DEPARTMENT:         deptCode(key), deptName, location

ENROLLMENT (bridge table for M:N):
  studentRollNo FK → STUDENT
  courseCode FK → COURSE
  enrollDate, grade

Converting ER to Relational Tables

1:1 Relationship:
  Add FK of either entity to the other (choose lower cardinality side)

1:N Relationship:
  Add FK of the "1" side to the "N" side table
  Teacher(teacherID, name) + Course(courseCode, title, teacherID_FK)

M:N Relationship:
  Create a new junction table with FKs from both sides
  Enrollment(studentID_FK, courseCode_FK, enrollDate, grade)
  Primary key of Enrollment = (studentID, courseCode)

Exam Q&A — Unit 3

Q1: Differentiate primary key, foreign key, candidate key with examples. (6 marks)

Answer: Primary key: uniquely identifies each tuple, not null (RollNo in Student). Candidate key: minimal super key, any could be primary (RollNo, Email, Phone — all unique). Foreign key: references primary key of another table, enforces referential integrity (DeptCode in Student references Department).

Q2: What is an ER diagram? Explain strong vs weak entities with example. (6 marks)

Answer: ER diagram is a graphical representation of entities, their attributes, and relationships. Strong entity: has its own primary key (Employee). Weak entity: depends on strong entity, has only partial key (Dependent — identified only in context of Employee). Weak entity represented by double rectangle, relationship by double diamond.

chapters.title: Unit 4: Dependencies & Normalization
chapters.content:
Unit 4: Database Dependencies and Normalization

6 Marks

Functional Dependencies

A functional dependency X → Y means: knowing X, you can always determine Y. (X functionally determines Y)

RollNo → Name, Marks, Department
  (Knowing roll number, you always know name/marks/dept uniquely)

ZipCode → City, State
  (Knowing zip code, you know city and state)

But: Name → RollNo is NOT valid (two students can have same name)

Types of Functional Dependencies

  • Trivial FD: Y ⊆ X. (e.g., {RollNo, Name} → RollNo). Always true, uninteresting.
  • Non-trivial FD: Y ⊄ X. Interesting, tells us something new.
  • Partial FD: Non-prime attribute depends on PART of composite key.
  • Transitive FD: A → B → C (A determines C through B)
STUDENT_COURSE(StudentID, CourseID, StudentName, CourseName, Grade)
Primary Key: (StudentID, CourseID)

Partial FDs:
  StudentID → StudentName  (part of key determines non-key attribute)
  CourseID → CourseName    (part of key determines non-key attribute)

Full FD (correct):
  (StudentID, CourseID) → Grade  (grade needs BOTH IDs to be determined)

Normalization

Normalization is the process of organizing a database to reduce redundancy and improve data integrity. It involves decomposing large tables into smaller, related tables.

Why Normalize? — Anomalies in Unnormalized Data

Unnormalized Table:
StudentID | StudentName | CourseID | CourseName | TeacherID | TeacherName
   101    |   Aayan    |  CS101   |   DSA      |    T1     |   Dr.Sharma
   101    |   Aayan    |  CS102   |   DBMS     |    T2     |   Dr.Verma
   102    |   Riya     |  CS101   |   DSA      |    T1     |   Dr.Sharma

Problems:
  INSERT anomaly: Can't add a course with no students enrolled yet
  UPDATE anomaly: Dr.Sharma's name in 2 places — if changed, must update all
  DELETE anomaly: If Aayan drops CS102, we lose T2/Dr.Verma information

First Normal Form (1NF)

Rule: All attributes must be atomic (single values, no repeating groups).

VIOLATION of 1NF:
  Student(RollNo, Name, Phones)  ← Phones can be multiple values
  
FIX (1NF):
  Student(RollNo, Name, Phone)   ← separate row for each phone
  Or: Student_Phone(RollNo, Phone) ← separate table

Second Normal Form (2NF)

Rule: Must be in 1NF + No partial dependencies (every non-key attribute must depend on the WHOLE primary key, not part of it).

VIOLATION of 2NF (table has composite key):
ENROLLMENT(StudentID, CourseID, StudentName, CourseName, Grade)
PK: (StudentID, CourseID)
  StudentID → StudentName  ← partial! StudentName depends on part of key
  CourseID → CourseName    ← partial!
  (StudentID, CourseID) → Grade ← full dependency ✓

FIX (2NF): Decompose into:
  STUDENT(StudentID, StudentName)
  COURSE(CourseID, CourseName)
  ENROLLMENT(StudentID, CourseID, Grade)  ← only full dependencies

Third Normal Form (3NF)

Rule: Must be in 2NF + No transitive dependencies (non-key attributes must not depend on other non-key attributes).

VIOLATION of 3NF:
EMPLOYEE(EmpID, EmpName, DeptID, DeptName, DeptLocation)
  EmpID → DeptID    (full dependency ✓)
  DeptID → DeptName, DeptLocation  ← TRANSITIVE! Non-key depends on non-key
  EmpID → DeptName  (through DeptID)

FIX (3NF): Decompose into:
  EMPLOYEE(EmpID, EmpName, DeptID)
  DEPARTMENT(DeptID, DeptName, DeptLocation)

Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF)

Rule: Must be in 3NF + For every FD X → Y, X must be a super key.

Example: STUDENT_COURSE(StudentID, CourseID, InstructorID)
  One instructor teaches one course (InstructorID → CourseID)
  One student can have multiple instructors for a course
  
  FD: InstructorID → CourseID, but InstructorID is NOT a super key!
  This violates BCNF (even though it's in 3NF).
  
FIX (BCNF): Decompose into:
  INSTRUCTOR_COURSE(InstructorID, CourseID)
  STUDENT_INSTRUCTOR(StudentID, InstructorID)

Exam Q&A — Unit 4

Q1: What is a functional dependency? Explain trivial vs non-trivial FD.

Answer: FD X→Y means X uniquely determines Y. Trivial: Y is subset of X (always true). Non-trivial: Y is not subset of X (meaningful new information). Example: {RollNo, Name}→RollNo is trivial; RollNo→Name is non-trivial.

Q2: Explain 1NF, 2NF, 3NF with examples. (8 marks)

Answer: 1NF: atomic attributes, no repeating groups. 2NF: 1NF + no partial dependencies (non-key attributes depend on whole PK). 3NF: 2NF + no transitive dependencies (non-key attributes don't depend on other non-key attributes). Each normal form builds on the previous and eliminates specific types of anomalies.

chapters.title: Unit 5: MySQL Overview
chapters.content:
Unit 5: Overview of MySQL

12 Marks

What is MySQL?

MySQL is the world's most popular open-source Relational Database Management System (RDBMS). It uses SQL (Structured Query Language) and is used by Facebook, Twitter, YouTube, WordPress, and countless web applications.

Key Features

  • Open source (free) with commercial edition available
  • Cross-platform (Windows, Linux, macOS)
  • ACID compliant (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability)
  • Supports multiple storage engines (InnoDB — default, MyISAM)
  • Replication and clustering for high availability

MySQL Data Types

Numeric Types

TypeRangeUse Case
TINYINT-128 to 127Boolean (0/1), small numbers
INT-2B to 2BIDs, counts, quantities
BIGINT±9 quintillionLarge IDs (Twitter post IDs)
FLOAT~7 decimal digitsApproximate decimals
DECIMAL(p,s)ExactFinancial data, marks

String Types

TypeStorageUse Case
CHAR(n)Fixed n bytesFixed-length: country code 'IN', gender 'M'
VARCHAR(n)Variable ≤ n bytesNames, emails, descriptions
TEXTUp to 65,535 bytesLong text: articles, comments
ENUM1-2 bytesFixed options: status ENUM('active','inactive')

Date/Time Types

TypeFormatUse Case
DATEYYYY-MM-DDBirthdays, deadlines
TIMEHH:MM:SSDuration, time of day
DATETIMEYYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SSTransactions, events
TIMESTAMPLike DATETIMEAuto-updates on row change
YEARYYYYYear of graduation

MySQL Operators

-- Arithmetic
SELECT 10 + 3, 10 - 3, 10 * 3, 10 / 3, 10 % 3;  -- 13, 7, 30, 3.33, 1

-- Comparison
SELECT * FROM Students WHERE marks > 60;      -- greater than
SELECT * FROM Students WHERE marks BETWEEN 60 AND 90;
SELECT * FROM Students WHERE name LIKE 'A%';   -- starts with A
SELECT * FROM Students WHERE name LIKE '%an';  -- ends with an
SELECT * FROM Students WHERE dept IN ('CS', 'IT', 'EC');

-- Logical
SELECT * FROM Students WHERE marks > 60 AND dept = 'CS';
SELECT * FROM Students WHERE marks > 90 OR dept = 'CS';
SELECT * FROM Students WHERE NOT dept = 'CS';

-- NULL handling
SELECT * FROM Students WHERE phone IS NULL;
SELECT * FROM Students WHERE phone IS NOT NULL;

MySQL System Schema & Privileges

-- Show all databases
SHOW DATABASES;

-- Show all tables in current DB
SHOW TABLES;

-- See table structure
DESCRIBE Students;  -- or DESC Students;

-- Create user
CREATE USER 'aayan'@'localhost' IDENTIFIED BY 'password123';

-- Grant privileges
GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON university.* TO 'aayan'@'localhost';
GRANT SELECT, INSERT ON university.Students TO 'viewer'@'%';

-- Revoke
REVOKE INSERT ON university.Students FROM 'viewer'@'%';

-- Show grants
SHOW GRANTS FOR 'aayan'@'localhost';

-- Drop user
DROP USER 'aayan'@'localhost';

Unit 6 Preview: SQL Query Language

Complete Query Examples

-- Create the database structure
CREATE DATABASE university;
USE university;

CREATE TABLE departments (
    dept_id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
    dept_name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    hod VARCHAR(50)
);

CREATE TABLE students (
    roll_no INT PRIMARY KEY,
    name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    email VARCHAR(100) UNIQUE,
    marks DECIMAL(5,2),
    dept_id INT,
    joined_year YEAR,
    FOREIGN KEY (dept_id) REFERENCES departments(dept_id)
);

-- Insert data
INSERT INTO departments (dept_name, hod) VALUES
    ('Computer Science', 'Dr. Sharma'),
    ('Information Technology', 'Dr. Verma'),
    ('Electronics', 'Dr. Gupta');

INSERT INTO students VALUES
    (101, 'Aayan Parmar', 'aayan@hpu.ac.in', 95.50, 1, 2023),
    (102, 'Riya Kapoor', 'riya@hpu.ac.in', 88.00, 1, 2023),
    (103, 'Arjun Singh', 'arjun@hpu.ac.in', 72.50, 2, 2022),
    (104, 'Priya Sharma', 'priya@hpu.ac.in', 45.00, 3, 2023),
    (105, 'Rahul Dev', 'rahul@hpu.ac.in', 91.00, 2, 2022);

-- Queries
-- 1. All students with marks above 80
SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE marks > 80 ORDER BY marks DESC;

-- 2. Count students per department
SELECT d.dept_name, COUNT(s.roll_no) AS total_students, AVG(s.marks) AS avg_marks
FROM departments d
LEFT JOIN students s ON d.dept_id = s.dept_id
GROUP BY d.dept_id, d.dept_name;

-- 3. Students above department average
SELECT name, marks FROM students s
WHERE marks > (SELECT AVG(marks) FROM students WHERE dept_id = s.dept_id);

-- 4. Students ordered by marks, highest first
SELECT roll_no, name, marks,
       RANK() OVER (ORDER BY marks DESC) AS rank_num
FROM students;

-- 5. String functions
SELECT UPPER(name), LENGTH(name), SUBSTRING(email, 1, INSTR(email,'@')-1) AS username
FROM students;

-- 6. Date functions
SELECT name, joined_year, YEAR(CURDATE()) - joined_year AS years_in_college
FROM students;

-- 7. HAVING (filter after GROUP BY)
SELECT dept_id, AVG(marks) AS avg_marks
FROM students
GROUP BY dept_id
HAVING avg_marks > 80;

-- 8. UNION (combine two queries)
SELECT name, 'High Performer' AS category FROM students WHERE marks >= 90
UNION
SELECT name, 'Average' FROM students WHERE marks >= 60 AND marks < 90
UNION
SELECT name, 'Needs Improvement' FROM students WHERE marks < 60;

Important SQL Functions

-- Aggregate
COUNT(*), SUM(col), AVG(col), MAX(col), MIN(col)

-- String
UPPER(str), LOWER(str), LENGTH(str), SUBSTRING(str, pos, len)
CONCAT(str1, str2), TRIM(str), REPLACE(str, old, new)
LPAD(str, len, pad), RPAD(str, len, pad)
LEFT(str, n), RIGHT(str, n), LTRIM(str), RTRIM(str)

-- Numeric
ROUND(n, d), FLOOR(n), CEIL(n), ABS(n), POWER(base, exp)
SQRT(n), MOD(n, d), TRUNCATE(n, d)

-- Date
NOW(), CURDATE(), CURTIME()
DATE_FORMAT(date, '%d/%m/%Y')
DATEDIFF(date1, date2)
DATE_ADD(date, INTERVAL 7 DAY)
YEAR(date), MONTH(date), DAY(date)

-- Conversion
CAST(col AS CHAR), CAST(col AS INT)
STR_TO_DATE(str, format)

Exam Q&A — Units 5 & 6

Q1: Write SQL to create a student table with appropriate constraints.

Answer: See CREATE TABLE students above. Key constraints: PRIMARY KEY (roll_no), UNIQUE (email), NOT NULL (name), DECIMAL for marks precision, FOREIGN KEY linking to departments.

Q2: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?

Answer: WHERE filters rows BEFORE grouping (on individual rows). HAVING filters groups AFTER GROUP BY (on aggregated results). Example: WHERE marks > 60 filters students; HAVING AVG(marks) > 60 filters department groups.

Q3: Explain INNER JOIN, LEFT JOIN, RIGHT JOIN with examples.

Answer: INNER JOIN: only matching rows from both tables. LEFT JOIN: all rows from left table + matching from right (NULLs for no match). RIGHT JOIN: all from right + matching from left. Example: LEFT JOIN departments to students shows departments even with no students enrolled.
